body: {"total":5,"records":[{"title":"Time from verification to notification of critical laboratory values: an eleven-laboratory analysis of 96,400 call-log entries","authors":"Petrosyan-Hale D, Obi-Lindstrom K, Varga-Ashby M","year":2020,"venue":"Caddisford Laboratory Practice Journal","doi":"10.5555/jlmp.2020.0318","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We analysed laboratory information system call logs for 96,400 critical values from eleven hospital laboratories over one year. Median time from verification to documented read-back was 7 minutes for inpatients and 24 minutes for outpatients. Notification within 30 minutes was achieved for 94 percent of inpatient results and 71 percent of outpatient results. Outpatient results verified after 17:00 had the longest delays, and 3 percent of outpatient critical values had no successful notification documented. Results requiring three or more call attempts accounted for most delays beyond one hour. Laboratories with a written escalation route for unreachable clinicians had shorter outpatient times."},{"title":"Unsuccessful call attempts and read-back documentation in critical value reporting at a regional laboratory","authors":"Sandoval-Nkosi T, Ekberg-Fairley A","year":2018,"venue":"Clinical Laboratory Operations","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We reviewed 8,200 critical value notifications from one regional laboratory. Eighteen percent of results needed more than two call attempts before a responsible clinician was reached, most often for outpatient and community results. Read-back was not documented for 9 percent of successful calls, more often at night. Call attempts were logged reliably, but the reason a call failed was recorded as free text in fewer than half of cases. The authors recommend structured fields for failed calls and a defined escalation after the second unsuccessful attempt."},{"title":"Timeliness, read-back and escalation in critical value notification: a systematic review of 31 laboratory studies","authors":"Halvorsen-Oduya B, Castell-Mbeki R, Tan-Whitaker J","year":2022,"venue":"Reviews in Laboratory Service Quality","doi":"10.5555/lmr.2022.0114","providerType":"review","abstract":"We included 31 studies of critical value notification from hospital and reference laboratories. Delays were consistently longer for outpatient and community results and outside working hours. Written escalation pathways were associated with shorter notification times in eight of nine studies that examined them. Studies defined timeliness differently: some measured from specimen collection, some from verification and some from the first call attempt, which made comparison difficult. Read-back documentation ranged from 78 to 99 percent. Only two studies linked notification delay to patient outcomes, both with small numbers of adverse events."},{"title":"Automated secure messaging versus telephone for critical value notification: a before-after comparison","authors":"Moreau-Adjei L, Kristoffersen-Iqbal S","year":2024,"venue":"Clinical Laboratory Operations","doi":"10.5555/clo.2024.0045","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"One hospital laboratory replaced telephone calls for selected critical values with secure messages requiring acknowledgement in the electronic record. Median time from verification to acknowledgement fell from 14 to 6 minutes. However, 12 percent of messages were not acknowledged within 30 minutes and had to be followed by a telephone call, and acknowledgement did not always mean that the clinician had read the result. The change applied only to inpatients and was accompanied by staff training. The authors caution that messaging needs a fallback call and should not be introduced for community results without an escalation route."},{"title":"Community clinic critical values after hours: who is responsible when the clinic is closed?","authors":"Regional Laboratory Quality Committee","year":2021,"venue":"Regional laboratory quality reports","providerType":"report","abstract":"This report describes how six laboratories handled critical values for community clinic patients verified after the clinic had closed. Laboratories could not reach a responsible clinician for 23 percent of such results on the first evening, mainly because on-call lists were out of date or not held by the laboratory. Staff then called the patient directly, contacted an emergency department or waited until the next morning, with no consistent rule. The committee recommends that every community clinic name an after-hours contact and that laboratories hold a current list, with a defined route when nobody can be reached."}]}
